---
title: "Step 3: Policy Scenarios"
---

## Overview

The Policy Scenarios step evaluates how specific adaptation interventions would change the welfare distribution produced in Step 2. The core of this work comprises the re-running of the welfare simulations and visualizations in Step 2, but with additional counterfactuals constructed by changing  household or area characteristics in the selectecd survey for simulation according to desired policy scenarios. 

Hence, one should refer back to the Step 2 page for a more detailed understanding of the simulation methodology and standard visualization output interpretations. The standard results output in Step 3 are identical to those described in Step 2, except with the additional policy-adjusted scenario output presented alongside all prior baseline and alternative climate scenarios.

Nevertheless, once simulated, Step 3 extends analysis of welfare simulation outputs in decompositional analysis. As underlying survey data is run with counterfactual characteristics on the Model in Step 1, changes to welfare can occur both at the level of distribution (i.e. households as richer or poorer with cash differing levels of assistance, infrastructure), as well as resiliance (i.e. households as they get richer may be less sensitive to changing weather conditions). This decomposition of welfare impact sources can further inform policy programming.

**For all non-cash tranfer policies, these policies MUST be included, ideally as interaction terms, in the defined Weather-Welfare Model defined in Step 1.**

## Instructions

The core of Step 3 comprises policy options to simulate how differing household and area characteristics would change welfare outcomes as observed in Step 2 based on the welfare-weather relationship defined in Step 1. The current iteration of the WISE-APP enables policy across five categories: Social Protection, Infrastructure, Digital Inclusion, Labor Market, and Education. Social Protection enables the most options, as it comprises cash transfer program settings. The remaining categories are simpler in implementation, typically with an option to change the proportion of a variable like educational attainment or access to electricity across the input survey by a margin (up to universal coverage), to simulate the impact of this policy change on welfare outcomes and the resulting sensitivity to differing climate scenarios.

How this setting is adjusted depends significantly on the policy variable selected. 

- **Binary Variables**: [Many policy variables are binaries (does the household have access to electricity, or have a member who attained at least a secondary school education, etc.). These binary variables can be adjusted to increase the proportion of households reporting these characteristics from -20% to +100%, by randomly selecting households to flip these attributes to meet the overall threshold. These variables will also have a universal coverage option, enabling a shift of all households to have coverage.]{.mark}

- **Numeric Variables**: [Some policy variables are numeric (i.e. reporting distance to nearest health centers, in minutes). These variables have a -20% to 100% option as well, which reduces all households numeric values by that amount. These variables may also have a maximum or minimum threshold value, operating similar to the universal coverage option, where all households exceeding the threshold values are replaced by that threshold.]{.mark}

Cash transfer approaches function somewhat differently, and are described in detail in the Social Protection section.

### Social Protection

Configure a cash transfer programme to eligible households.

#### Programme type

The current iteration of the WISE-APP enbles only a regular chash transfer option, one that runs regardless of weather conditions. 

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
#### Potential Future Adjustments
Another possibility would be to develop a 'shock-response' program, which would activate only after a set trigger. This could include:

- **Return period of event ≥ x years** (default: 10) — the programme activates when the weather event has a return period of at least x years (i.e. a 1-in-x year event or worse).
- **Weather variable exceeds x** — the programme activates when a specific weather variable surpasses a numeric threshold.
- **Modelled welfare loss ≥ $x** — the programme activates when the model predicts that average welfare will fall by at least $x.
- **Modelled increase in poverty gap ≥ $x** — the programme activates when the model predicts the poverty gap will increase by at least $x.

:::

#### Budget and transfer amount

Two budget modes are available:

- **Transfer-first** (default) — specify the transfer amount per household ($/HH); the total programme budget is derived from the number of beneficiaries.
- **Budget-first** — specify the total programme budget; the per-household transfer is derived from the number of beneficiaries. Budget can be set as a fixed amount, a share of modelled welfare loss, a proportion of the poverty increase, or based on the annual expected loss.


#### Targeting

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
#### Potential Future Adjustments
Another possibility would be to develop a 'PMT for modeling cash assistance approaches, this would require an expansion of the categorial targeting approach defined below.
:::

Select which households receive the transfer:

- **Universal** — all households receive the transfer.
- **Ex-ante poor** (default) — households below the welfare threshold in the survey (bottom 20% by default). The poorest percentile cutoff is adjustable (5–60%).
- **Categorical Targeting** — households identified by individual demographic or area characteristics.

For all non-universal targeting methods, specify:

- **Inclusion error** (default 10%) — the share of non-eligible households incorrectly included in the programme.
- **Exclusion error** (default 10%) — the share of eligible households incorrectly excluded.


#### Frequency and Timing

For regular programmes, specify the number of transfer payments per year (default: 6, from 2-24 times per year an option).

### Infrastructure

Current infrastructure variables are:

- Households reporting access to electricity
- Households reporting access to piped water
- Households reporting access to a health care facility

For access to electricity or piped water, there are options to change the access by a percentage range (-20% to 100%) as well as an option to provide universal coverage. 

For access to health facilities, one can change travel time as a percentage change from baseline (-20% to +100%), or set a maximum travel time (in minutes).

### Digital Inclusion

Current digital inclusion variables are:

- Internet access
- Mobile phone ownership

As binary variables, these can be adjusted to universal coverage or as a percentage change from baseline (-20% to +100%). [For percentage changes, a randome fraction of those households are selected and changed to match that percentage.]{.mark}

### Running the Policy Simulation

Once the policy parameters are set, click **Run simulation**. WISE-APP re-runs the Step 2 simulation with the modified household and area characteristics, producing a counterfactual welfare distribution that can be compared directly against the Step 2 baseline.

## Results

The results and adjustment settings on the results tab will be identical in layout and options to what was displayed in Step 2, and the policy simulation will be interpreted identically as an alternative counterfactual as compared to a baseline or alternative weather scenario. Please refer to Step 2 guidance for further details and context for how to interpret these charts.

## Diagnostics

The diagnostics tabs in the policy scenario option provides some basic summary statistics and descriptives on the policy veriable of interest, and how it affects the welfare outcome of interest.

## Decomposition

WISE-APP decomposes the total effect of a policy intervention into two channels: the **main effect** (direct welfare change) and the **resilience effect** (change in weather sensitivity). This tab presents an overview of these effects, but it is crucial to understand the terms used here. Understanding this decomposition helps distinguish policies that raise welfare levels from those that reduce vulnerability to weather variability — and from those that do both.

### Main Effect

The main effect captures the direct welfare change attributable to the policy, holding weather conditions constant. It has two components:

1. **Cash transfer effect** — for social protection programmes, the direct income boost to eligible households. The transfer raises welfare regardless of weather conditions.

2. **Covariate shift effect** — for infrastructure, digital, and labour market policies, the welfare change associated with the modified covariate itself. For example, gaining access to electricity is associated with higher welfare, as captured by the electricity coefficient in the Step 1 model. This represents the average welfare gain from the policy at observed weather conditions.

The main effect shifts the welfare exceedance curve upward (or, for poverty indicators, leftward) — it raises welfare outcomes regardless of what the weather is doing in a given year.

### Resilience Effect

The resilience effect captures how the policy changes the *relationship* between weather and welfare. A policy with a positive resilience effect makes welfare less responsive to weather shocks — it flattens the exceedance curve rather than simply shifting it.

The resilience effect has two sub-channels:

**Interaction channel.** When the policy changes a covariate that also appears in a weather × covariate interaction in the Step 1 model, the policy changes the effective weather coefficient for affected households. For example, if temperature is interacted with electricity access in Step 1, then increasing electricity access reduces the temperature coefficient for newly electrified households — they become less sensitive to heat stress. This channel is present for both linear and distributional regression engines.

**Repositioning channel** (distributional regression only). This channel is unique to the RIF regression engine. When the welfare distribution has heterogeneous weather sensitivity — poor households are more vulnerable to weather than wealthy ones — any policy that raises a household's welfare also changes its position in the distribution and, with it, its weather vulnerability. A cash transfer that lifts a household from the 10th to the 25th percentile moves it to a part of the distribution with lower weather sensitivity, even without changing any observable household characteristic. This indirect resilience effect of income support is captured automatically when distributional regression is used in Step 1. It is not present in linear regression results.

### The Decomposition Tab

The Decomposition tab reports, for each household or welfare decile:

- **Main effect** — direct welfare change, broken down into cash transfer and covariate shift components.
- **Resilience effect** — change in weather sensitivity, broken down into interaction and repositioning components.
- **Total effect** — the sum of main and resilience effects.

Effects are reported both in welfare units and as percentage changes. The channel totals reconcile with the exceedance curve results in the Results tab.

::: {.callout-note}
## How the regression engine affects policy results

The choice of regression engine in Step 1 has important consequences for policy analysis in Step 3:

**Linear regression** can only produce a resilience effect through the interaction channel. The modified covariate must appear in an interaction with a weather variable in the Step 1 specification. Cash transfers that raise income have no resilience effect in a linear model unless a cash × weather interaction is explicitly included — which is uncommon. As a result, the resilience effects of social protection programmes tend to be understated.

**Distributional regression (RIF)** captures resilience through both the interaction channel and the repositioning channel. Cash transfers automatically build resilience by shifting poor households to less weather-vulnerable parts of the welfare distribution, even without any interaction term. This is the more complete measure of total resilience, particularly for poverty-focused analyses.

When comparing policy effects across engine choices, expect the RIF engine to show larger total resilience effects, especially for cash transfer and social protection programmes.
:::

### Limitations

**Model-conditional effects.** All policy effects are conditional on the Step 1 model. A policy that targets a covariate not included in the model — or included as a main effect without an interaction — will produce only a main effect, even if the true policy also reduces weather sensitivity.

**No general equilibrium.** The simulation modifies household-level characteristics but treats the broader economic environment (prices, wages, labour demand) as fixed. Policies with economy-wide effects may be under- or overstated.

**Extrapolation from the training data.** The policy simulation applies Step 1 coefficients to a modified survey. If the policy moves households to covariate values rarely or never observed in the training data (for example, near-universal electrification in a survey with low baseline access), the coefficients estimated from the observed data may not accurately represent welfare outcomes in that counterfactual regime.

## 3.6 Interpreting Results

Results show the policy's impact on two dimensions, displayed as overlaid exceedance curves (baseline vs. policy counterfactual):

- **Welfare level** — a vertical shift of the exceedance curve indicates a direct change in average welfare. An upward shift (for welfare) or leftward shift (for poverty) means households are better off on average under the policy.
- **Weather sensitivity / resilience** — a change in the slope of the exceedance curve indicates that the relationship between weather and welfare has changed. A flatter curve under the policy means households are less exposed to weather-driven welfare swings — i.e. the policy improves resilience.

**How policies work in the model:**

- **Infrastructure, digital, and labour market policies** modify the covariate values for affected households. The welfare change is computed through the regression coefficients estimated in Step 1. If a variable appears in an interaction term with a weather variable (Step 1, interaction settings), changing it will also change the weather sensitivity of welfare — this is how these policies produce resilience effects.
- **Social protection policies** add a direct income transfer to eligible households, shifting their welfare upward by the transfer amount. When triggered by weather events, the transfer partially offsets weather-driven welfare losses.

::: {.callout-note}
## Development status
Infrastructure, digital inclusion, and labour market scenario results are available in the current release. The full social protection simulation — including trigger activation, targeting errors, and budget mechanics — is under active development.
:::

## Tips and Common Issues

- **Tip:** A policy that flattens the exceedance curve without shifting its level indicates a pure resilience effect — the policy does not change average welfare but reduces exposure to weather extremes. This is a distinct and valuable outcome for climate adaptation.
- **Tip:** Compare the resilience effects of different policy types. Infrastructure and digital policies tend to reduce weather sensitivity when the relevant variables appear in interaction terms in Step 1; labour market policies shift the sectoral composition and can affect exposure to weather shocks differently.
- **Tip:** Run multiple policies individually before combining them. This allows you to attribute the combined effect to its components.
- **Issue:** If a policy produces no change in weather sensitivity, check whether the modified variable was included as an interaction term in Step 1. Variables that only enter the model as main-effect covariates will shift the welfare level but not the slope of the exceedance curve.
- **Issue:** Policy effects are conditional on the Step 1 model specification. Policies that target variables not present in the survey data, or not selected as covariates, will have no effect in the simulation.

Labor Market Indicators
Modify aggregate labour market conditions by specifying changes in percentage points from the survey baseline:

- **Labour force participation** — change in pp (−20 to +20 pp, default 0).
- **Employment rate** — change in pp (−20 to +20 pp, default 0).
- **Sectoral composition** — shift toward agriculture, manufacturing, or services.
